prayer.text: Saints Nereus and Achilleus, pray for us.

cues.text: Soldiers of the Guard

Nereus and Achilleus were, by ancient tradition, soldiers of the Roman imperial guard — some accounts identify them as eunuch chamberlains in the service of Flavia Domitilla, a Christian noblewoman of the imperial family exiled for her faith under Domitian.
An epitaph composed by Pope Damasus I , who took a personal interest in recording the memory of Rome's ancient martyrs, describes the two men as having 'carried out the cruel orders of the tyrant.'
A sudden conversion then changed the course of their lives entirely.
A Sudden Conversion
Damasus's epitaph records that Nereus and Achilleus abruptly renounced their military service after their conversion to Christ.
They threw down their shields, armor, and spears rather than continue serving 'the camp of their evil leader'—an image of decisive rejection of military service for the sake of the Gospel.
This made a deep impression on later generations of the Roman Church.
Martyrdom and Burial
The two are traditionally held to have been martyred by beheading, likely under Domitian or during a later persecution.
Their bodies were buried together in what became known as the Catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina, a name recalling the Christian noblewoman with whom their story is entwined.
Excavations there in the nineteenth century uncovered a fourth-century basilica built over their tomb, along with sculpted images associated with their martyrdom.
Honored in the Roman Mass
From the earliest surviving Roman liturgical calendars, Nereus and Achilleus were commemorated jointly on May 12.
Their names were entered together in ancient Roman liturgical books for the Mass of their feast, reflecting a tradition of veneration documented in the fourth-century Roman calendar.
Even so, as the Catholic Encyclopedia notes, the surviving legendary Acts describing their lives have little independent historical value.
Legacy
Their statues today stand among the many saints represented in the colonnade of St. Peter's Square in Rome.
Their joint feast — still kept as an optional memorial on the General Roman Calendar — preserves the memory of two soldiers whose conversion led them to abandon violence for Christ.
This image has resonated with Christians who see their story as a witness to rejecting military service for the sake of Christ.
